content.title: About
content.content: Eggplant is the fruit of the plant Solanum melongena, belonging to the nightshade family. Raw eggplant has a smooth, glossy dark‑purple skin, tender flesh, and a mildly bitter flavor. It is used worldwide in cuisine, both fresh and after cooking.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Eggplant was first domesticated in India and China over 2,000 years ago.
It is a close relative of tomatoes, potatoes, and peppers.
The deep purple skin is due to anthocyanins, powerful antioxidants.
In Japan it is called "nasu," and in Turkey it is known as "patlıcan."
There are more than 300 varieties, differing in shape, size, and color.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Anthocyanins and vitamin C help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports heart health
items.content: Low calorie content and fiber help lower cholesterol levels.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Eggplant provides vitamin B6, niacin, and folate, important for metabolism.

items.title: May help regulate blood sugar
items.content: Its low glycemic index assists in maintaining stable glucose levels after meals.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience an allergic reaction to eggplant.

items.title: Oxalate content
items.content: Eggplant contains oxalates, which in excess can contribute to kidney stone formation.

items.title: Bitterness
items.content: Certain varieties may have a stronger bitter taste that not everyone enjoys.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Raw eggplant can be sliced thinly and added to salads, pickled, used in rolls, or served as a cold appetizer. Before eating, it is common to sprinkle the slices with salt, let them sit for 15‑20 minutes to draw out bitterness, then rinse.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store eggplant in the refrigerator’s vegetable drawer, wrapped in a paper towel or a perforated bag. When kept properly, it stays fresh for 5‑7 days. Avoid very low temperatures, which can cause the texture to deteriorate.
